# Software Architecture and Microservice Workshop

*Building effective software efficiently*

## Split the modular monolithic application into multiple projects

This architectural style takes the modular monolith approach and separates each
module into an independent project. The refactoring process itself is not
covered here; however, it can be carried out through a series of defined steps,
as outlined below.

![Extracting each component as separate projects](./assets/images/Extracting%20each%20component%20as%20separate%20projects.png)

Please note that this is quite a small project, and it does not usually warrant
such a split. As discussed in the previous section, splitting the project into
smaller ones adds to the overhead and in this case may not be justified.

> **So why are we splitting it?**
>
> We are splitting this project into smaller projects each having its own
> repository to first show how this refactoring can be undertaken and also to
> provide a platform to discuss the challenges of such undertaking.

Our project comprises two features, catalogue and cart, and a common project.
These three will be moved into three distinct projects. We will take the first
grow and then shrink approach. The current project contains the whole
application. We will start by copying the whole project, and then we will remove
anything that is not needed, hence grown and then shrink. This will be described
in detail as we start the refactoring.

### Architecture Decision Records (ADR)

We are dividing the single project into multiple projects, each maintained in
its own repository. This architectural decision should be documented in an
Architecture Decision Record (ADR).

The initial layered monolithic architecture style defined in `ADR-005` was
superseded by the modular monolithic architecture style outlined in `ADR-006`.
This ADR takes the approach a step further by dividing the single project into
multiple projects. `ADR-006` is now superseded by `ADR-007` and should be updated to
reflect this change.

Lastly, update the `README.md` file, which summarises all ADRs, to clearly
indicate that ADR-006 has been superseded by ADR-007.

### Test the application

Please note that this architectural change does not modify the underlying
business logic. The business logic remains exactly as it was, without any
alterations.

Build the application and run the tests

```shell
./mvnw clean verify
```

Try the application now that all four components are extracted into separate
projects.

```shell
# Start the application in the background
java -jar './application/target/application-monolithic-modular-multi-project-application-1.0.0.jar' > './application/target/modular-multi-project-monolithic-architecture.log' 2>&1 &

# Save the PID so later steps can reuse it after this entry finishes.
echo "$!" > './application/target/application-monolithic-modular-multi-project-application.pid'

# Wait for the application to start
while [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:8080/cart/1')" -ne '200' ]; do echo 'Waiting for the application to start'; sleep 1; done
```

This starts our application in the background and waits until it is ready to
handle requests. The application is now running on localhost and listening on
port `8080`.

Make a few requests to the catalogue items endpoint. We have the following
catalogue items in the database.

| `id` | `caption`     | `description`                                                         |
| ---: | ------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
|    1 | Leather Sofa  | A very nice and comfortable sofa                                      |
|    2 | Wooden Table  | A large table ideal for 6 to 8 people                                 |
|    3 | Plastic Chair | A robust plastic chair ideal for children and adults alike            |
|    4 | Mug           | The ideal way to start the day                                        |
|    5 | LED TV        | A very large TV set, ideal for those who love to binge-watch TV shows |

Request the details for the item with id `1`.

```shell
curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/catalogue/item/1' | jq
```

The catalogue item with id `1`

```json
{
  "id": 1,
  "caption": "Leather Sofa",
  "description": "A very nice and comfortable sofa"
}
```

Add a new item to the catalogue.

We will add a new item named `Green Plant`, with the description:
`Put a little life in your living room!`. The response will then be saved to a
file so that we can use the generated id to retrieve the item later.

```shell
# Save the response in a file as we will use it later on
curl --silent \
  -X POST 'http://localhost:8080/catalogue/item' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"caption":"Green Plant","description":"Put a little life in your living room!!"}' \
  | jq \
  > new-catalogue-item.json

# Print the output
jq . new-catalogue-item.json
```

The newly added item

```json
{
  "id": 6,
  "caption": "Green Plant",
  "description": "Put a little life in your living room!!"
}
```

Fetch this item using the generated id.

```shell
# Read the new item id obtained from the previous command
ITEM_ID="$(jq .id new-catalogue-item.json)"

# Fetch the new item
curl --silent "http://localhost:8080/catalogue/item/${ITEM_ID}" | jq
```

The newly added item

```json
{
  "id": 6,
  "caption": "Green Plant",
  "description": "Put a little life in your living room!!"
}
```

The database has three carts, as shown in the following table.

| `cart_id` | `item_id` | `caption`     | `quantity` |
| --------: | --------: | ------------- | ---------: |
|         1 |         1 | Leather Sofa  |          1 |
|         1 |         5 | LED TV        |          1 |
|         2 |         2 | Wooden Table  |          1 |
|         2 |         3 | Plastic Chair |          6 |
|         3 |         4 | Mug           |          4 |

Request the details for the cart with id `1`.

```shell
curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/cart/1' | jq
```

The cart with id `1` and its items

```json
{
  "id": 1,
  "items": [
    {
      "id": 1,
      "caption": "Leather Sofa",
      "quantity": 1
    },
    {
      "id": 5,
      "caption": "LED TV",
      "quantity": 1
    }
  ]
}
```

Add the new item to the cart.

```shell
# Read the new item id obtained from the previous command
ITEM_ID="$(jq .id new-catalogue-item.json)"

# Add the new item to cart with id 1
curl --silent -X POST "http://localhost:8080/cart/1/item/${ITEM_ID}" | jq
```

The cart contents after adding the newly created catalogue item.

```json
{
  "id": 1,
  "items": [
    {
      "id": 1,
      "caption": "Leather Sofa",
      "quantity": 1
    },
    {
      "id": 5,

      "id": 6,
```

Delete the temporary file `new-catalogue-item.json`, which was created to store
the id of the newly added item to the catalogue.

```shell
rm -rf new-catalogue-item.json
```

Stop the application once ready.

```shell
kill "$(cat './application/target/application-monolithic-modular-multi-project-application.pid')"
rm -f './application/target/application-monolithic-modular-multi-project-application.pid'
```

### Containers

As with the previous architectural approach, this JAR file may be packaged
within a container. In this example, we will use `jlink`, assuming the JAR file
has already been generated. For a full reference implementation, see
[`./containers/Dockerfile`](./containers/Dockerfile). Once completed, you can
build the container using this optimised method.

```shell
docker build \
  --file './containers/Dockerfile' \
  --tag 'demo:application-monolithic-modular-multi-project' \
  --load \
  .
```

The only thing that changed from the first example is the Docker file.

Try the catalogue and cart features in the application

```shell
# Start the application in the background
docker run \
  --rm \
  --detach \
  --name 'application-monolithic-modular-multi-project' \
  --publish 8080:8080 \
  'demo:application-monolithic-modular-multi-project'

# Wait for the application to start
while [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:8080/cart/1')" -ne '200' ]; do echo 'Waiting for the application to start'; sleep 1; done
```

This starts our application in the background and waits until it is ready to
handle requests. The application is now running on localhost and listening on
port `8080`.

### Tradeoffs

A **single large repository (monorepo)** provides strong consistency and
simplifies dependency management. With one codebase, teams can make atomic
changes across components, ensuring the **cart, catalogue, and fulfilment** stay
in sync. Shared tooling, libraries, and coding standards are easier to enforce,
and visibility across the system promotes collaboration. Organisations like
Google leverage monorepos with sophisticated tooling to handle scale, enabling
global refactors and consistent builds across thousands of projects.

By contrast, a **multi-repository setup** offers clearer ownership and autonomy.
Each repo can have its own release cycle, pipeline, and technology stack, making
it easier for independent teams to evolve their services at their own pace. For
example, the **cart** team can release multiple times a day without waiting for
the **catalogue** team. Multi-repos also reduce the cognitive load of navigating
a massive codebase and can limit the blast radius of risky changes.

However, both approaches come with limitations. Monorepos without strong tooling
can become unwieldy, with long build times and frequent merge conflicts. They
can also blur ownership boundaries, as every team works in the same space.
Multi-repos, meanwhile, introduce challenges with
**cross-service changes, version drift, and dependency management**, making
integration between **cart, catalogue, and fulfilment** more complex. In
practice, the best choice depends on the organisation’s size and tooling
maturity: monorepos excel with strong automation and shared infrastructure,
while multi-repos suit teams optimising for autonomy and service isolation.

Splitting each domain (cart, catalogue, fulfilment) into its own repository
enforces strong ownership boundaries and autonomy, but introduces coordination
overhead. Adding a new catalogue attribute consumed by the cart might require
synchronising changes across two repos and pipelines, reducing lead time (3/5)
and ease of change (3/5) compared to a single-repo modular monolith.

Deployment frequency (3/5) is possible per repo, but in practice teams often
must coordinate releases when modules interact. Similarly, the change failure
rate (3/5) remains moderate: repo separation reduces coupling, but version drift
and integration risks offset some of the gains. MTTR (3/5) is affected by more
complex rollback and testing across multiple build pipelines.

For developers, cognitive load (2/5) increases because they must manage multiple
repositories, pipelines, and dependencies. A developer making a change to
cart-fulfilment integration must juggle two repos, which slows work.
Satisfaction (3/5) reflects this mixed experience: autonomy is higher, but
friction also grows. Communication (3/5) is more challenging than in a single
repo, as changes span multiple pipelines and require coordination between teams.

#### All or nothing

We have now introduced more moving parts, as listed below

- `application`
- `cart`
- `catalogue`
- `common`
- `db-migration`

The monolithic application needs to be built and compiled as a whole despite the
multiple projects. This requires coordination between all the projects
(*components*) which introduces new risks and complexities. Each project has its
own repository and its own build pipeline. The artefact (JAR file) produced by
each project needs to be saved in a central repository from where the other
projects can access it. Once a project is changed, all the components that
depend on it must be rebuilt. This adds complexity to the build pipeline.

That’s why I deducted the score for most of the questions. This refactoring
added complexity without providing any benefits. While this is a small example,
many projects tend to get overengineered without gaining anything. Please be
mindful of what’s being “paid” in contrast to what’s being “gained”. One of your
roles as an architect is to balance the tradeoffs and making sure that you are
not paying more than you should.
